name: Isfahan Metro
description: Isfahan Metro provides a north–south urban rail corridor through central Isfahan, linking Qods with the southern Soffeh area. Its operating Line 1 and the development of Line 2 illustrate the distinction between completing infrastructure and establishing a passenger service.

seo.title: Isfahan Metro: Operating Corridor and Network Development | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Isfahan Metro’s north–south corridor, phased development and the evidence separating Line 2 construction from passenger operations.

content.heading: A railway through the city
content.content:
Isfahan Metro is an urban rapid-transit system, distinct from the national railway used for intercity journeys. Its principal operating corridor crosses the city from Qods in the north towards Defa-e Moqaddas, also known as Soffeh, in the south. A report quoting the operating company’s chief executive described Line 1 as approximately 20 kilometres long, with 20 active stations. These are a dated description of the operating line, rather than measurements of every proposed extension. [s2]

The alignment helps explain the railway’s urban role. UrbanRail describes a route through the centre along Chaharbagh Boulevard, connecting the areas of the Kaveh and Soffeh intercity bus terminals. The metro therefore serves an internal city corridor while also bringing urban rail close to longer-distance road transport. This relationship does not make a metro ticket an intercity ticket, nor establish coordinated connections between the services. [s1]

content.heading: A line assembled in stages
content.content:
The railway emerged through successive openings. UrbanRail’s chronology records the Qods–Shohada section opening in October 2015, an extension to Takhti in November 2016, a further extension to Azadi in July 2017, and the southern extension to Soffeh in July 2018. Its record also identifies stations added within previously opened sections. A line’s inauguration date consequently does not establish that its eventual route and every station were available from the beginning. [s1]

The same source retains earlier construction expectations alongside later opening dates. This makes it useful for understanding the project’s evolution, but unsuitable as a stand-alone statement of today’s timetable. Its introductory narrative and detailed chronology also differ over the month of the initial opening; October follows the dated chronology and requires confirmation against an original operator record. [s1]

content.heading: Construction is not passenger operation
content.content:
In a report dated 8 Dey 1404 in the Iranian Solar Hijri calendar, municipal rail officials described Line 2 as an unfinished project running from the northeastern Darak area through central Isfahan towards Khomeinishahr. They said trial operation of an initial section depended on obtaining trains, with the national government and Interior Ministry responsible for fleet provision. The announced opening target was a prospective commitment, not evidence that service subsequently began. [s2]

A later transport-news report continued to describe Line 2 construction and identified Imam Hossein as the intended intersection with Line 1. It also reported efforts to reduce peak-hour intervals on the operating line. Read together, these accounts show why tracks, stations, trains and service frequency need separate treatment: progress in one does not automatically establish readiness in the others. A dated operator notice confirming the extent of public service is still needed before publishing a current transfer guide. [s3]

name: Air Transport
description: Iran’s air transport system combines airline operations, airports, air navigation and aircraft support services. Its development depends on the interaction between travel demand, available aircraft, infrastructure, regulatory permissions and international operating conditions.

seo.title: Air Transport in Iran: Networks, Capacity and Constraints | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: An evidence-based introduction to Iran’s aviation network, airport planning, fleet constraints and the limits of available traffic statistics.

content.heading: Demand and capacity must be considered together
content.content:
Iran’s aviation system cannot be understood simply by counting airports. A paper presented by Iran to the International Civil Aviation Organization, the United Nations agency responsible for international civil aviation standards, frames network planning around travel demand, fleet availability, route costs and airport configuration. It considers aviation alongside other transport modes rather than assuming that every journey should become a flight. [s1]

The paper contrasts a baseline constrained by the existing fleet with an optimistic scenario allowing aircraft additions and modernization. These are modelling assumptions, not observed outcomes or confirmed aircraft deliveries. Their practical significance is that infrastructure and aircraft supply must be assessed together: a proposed network can require capacity that the available fleet cannot provide. [s1]

content.heading: The services behind a flight
content.content:
Aircraft availability is only one part of operational continuity. In a draft report for its 2025 Assembly, ICAO’s Economic Commission summarized an Iranian submission describing constraints affecting procurement, maintenance, payments, insurance and workforce stability. The submission attributed these difficulties to unilateral economic sanctions and sought international action to protect civil aviation. This is evidence of Iran’s stated position; the summary does not independently quantify the effect of each constraint or establish their relative contribution to particular disruptions. [s2]

For readers exploring this subject, that distinction matters. Maintenance, airport handling, airline management and international payments are connected operational subjects, but they require different evidence. A claim about restricted access to equipment cannot by itself establish the airworthiness of a particular aircraft, while an airline’s advertised network does not demonstrate that each service operated. [s2]

content.heading: Connectivity can change faster than infrastructure
content.content:
Recent reporting illustrates the difference between a permanent airport and a continuously available route. In July 2025, the Associated Press reported a foreign flight arriving at Imam Khomeini airport following a suspension of international air travel, with further services expected to return gradually. That report documents a reopening episode, not uninterrupted operation afterwards. [s3]

On 18 April 2026, bne IntelliNews reported another reopening of airports and a resumption of commercial services after a wartime shutdown. Its account distinguished international schedules at Imam Khomeini from domestic traffic at Mehrabad and quoted an industry representative on the need for regulatory permits before additional flights could be scheduled. The report is a dated operational snapshot; it cannot establish the route network at the October research cutoff. [s4]

content.heading: What the available statistics establish
content.content:
The World Bank publishes an Iran series titled “Air transport, passengers carried,” identifying ICAO statistics and staff estimates as its sources. The inspected page displayed coverage through 2023 but did not expose the annual observations needed for a reproducible dataset in this research session. A numerical trend is therefore omitted. The page’s existence should not be treated as evidence that data for the cutoff year are available. [s5]

A complete account still requires verified annual observations, the indicator’s full scope and airport-level statistics with consistent reporting periods. Those additions would allow the reader to distinguish changes in airline activity from changes at individual airports, rather than treating every aviation total as interchangeable. [s5]

name: International Airports
description: Iran’s international airport infrastructure extends beyond Tehran to cities including Mashhad, Isfahan, Shiraz, Tabriz and Bandar Abbas. An airport’s inclusion in an international planning inventory does not establish the destinations, frequencies or passenger services available on a particular date.

seo.title: International Airports in Iran: Geography and Service Availability | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iran’s international airport geography and learn why airport designation, safety oversight and active flight schedules require separate evidence.

content.heading: A network beyond the capital
content.content:
The 2024 report of ICAO’s regional Aerodromes Safety, Planning and Implementation Group identifies Iranian airports in several parts of the country. Its monitoring material includes Imam Khomeini and Mehrabad in Tehran; Shahid Hashemi Nejad in Mashhad; Shahid Beheshti in Isfahan, also transliterated Esfahan; Shahid Dastghaib in Shiraz; and airports in Tabriz, Bandar Abbas, Yazd and Zahedan. These names help international readers recognize airports that may be presented under either a city name or a commemorative name. [s1]

The report is a regional infrastructure and safety-monitoring document. Its airport inventory is not a schedule of flights and should not be used to infer that every listed airport has continuous international passenger service. The meeting itself called for the monitored list to be updated against each state’s Aeronautical Information Publication, the official reference for published aeronautical information. [s1]

content.heading: An international airport is not a guaranteed international connection
content.content:
Historical operational material reinforces the need to distinguish an airport’s designation from its available services. The United States Federal Aviation Administration’s Iran entry in its International Flight Information Manual listed airports of entry at Tehran, Mashhad, Isfahan, Shiraz, Tabriz and Bandar Abbas, among others. However, that document is dated October 2014 and explicitly warns that its accuracy and currency are uncertain. It is useful as a historical reference, not a basis for current entry procedures or route availability. [s2]

The editorial consequence is straightforward: a current directory needs more than an airport name and code. It requires dated evidence of the services being described. Historical permission to receive international aircraft does not establish that an airline currently sells a route, that a scheduled departure operates, or that the airport is available without temporary restrictions. The FAA document’s own warning makes that limitation explicit. [s2]

content.heading: Tehran illustrates the operational distinction
content.content: A report by bne IntelliNews on 18 April 2026 described international schedules at Imam Khomeini airport while identifying domestic traffic at Mehrabad. This provides a dated example of different roles within the same metropolitan area; it is not evidence that the distribution of services remained unchanged through October. The same report described reopening after a wartime interruption, demonstrating that the continued existence of infrastructure and the availability of flights are separate questions. [s3]

content.heading: What remains necessary for a current guide
content.content: A reliable airport comparison must keep its evidence at the right scale. The inspected regional report supports identifying airports and understanding the purpose of infrastructure monitoring. The historical FAA manual supports a dated account of airports of entry. Neither supplies a verified current list of international destinations or a comparable annual traffic series. This page therefore retains the supported geography while withholding rankings, terminal-capacity claims and current route lists pending stronger evidence. [s1][s2]
